text: This is a tiny looped transformer, built from scratch on a MacBook. The question it explores: can an AI think longer, without getting bigger?

A normal transformer is a stack of layers. Each layer is one step of thinking. More steps make a smarter model, but every new layer brings its own new weights. So the model gets bigger, and more expensive.

A looped transformer takes a different route. A prelude reads the problem. Then one core layer runs again and again, with the same weights every time. Finally a coda gives the answer. More loops means more thinking, with zero extra parameters.

To test this, we built a puzzle: follow the arrows. Sixteen nodes, each pointing to exactly one other node. Start at node four, and follow five arrows. You cannot skip ahead, because every hop needs the one before it. We trained on up to four hops, and tested on up to eight.

We trained three models from scratch. Shallow, with two layers. Deep, with eight different layers and one point six million parameters. And looped, with about six hundred thousand parameters, whose depth grows with every loop we run.

Here are the results. Shallow fails after two hops. Deep solves up to four, then breaks. The looped model also solves four, and then solves five hops, which it never saw in training, at ninety six percent. With less than half the parameters of the deep model.
This heat map shows accuracy for every number of loops, and every number of hops. It forms a staircase. Each extra loop unlocks roughly one more hop. The loops really are reasoning steps.

We can also look inside. After each loop, we decode the model's hidden state. After loop one, it points at hop three. After loop two, hop four. After loop three, the answer. And then it holds it. The model is walking the path in its head.

But looping has a trap. A model trained with exactly four loops is perfect at four. Run it longer, and it gets worse, falling to thirty five percent at thirty two loops. It overthinks, and loses the answer. A model trained with random loop counts stays at one hundred percent.

We tested three cures. Multi step loss barely helped. Training with random loop counts fixed it. And a tiny write back gate, which lets each token say, I am done, fixed it too. Back to one hundred percent.

Sometimes, more loops even solve harder problems the model never saw. One gated model jumped from thirty seven to ninety five percent on five hops, just by thinking for sixteen loops instead of four. But this depended on the random seed. The model knows how to step, but not always when to stop.
Thinking longer is not free. Every loop costs time. Thirty two loops is about eleven times slower than one.
Here are the raw benchmark heat maps from every experiment: the baseline, the gate, multi step loss, and a second seed. Every number in this video comes from these runs.
So. Depth beats size. Loops are reasoning steps. And a looped model must learn when to stop. All the code and results are open source on GitHub.
